newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican union cut-price beans plan turns sour.
newsitem.headline: Mexican union cut-price beans plan turns sour.

text.p: Mexican bean growers claimed Wednesday they were double-crossed over price by the Mexican Workers' Confederation which foiled the plans of the country's top union movement to offer cut-price beans to members.

"We were promised one price and when we were about to deliver the beans we were offered another, we had no option but to refuse the deal," a spokesman for a group of Zacatecas state bean farmers told Reuters.
Farmers, mainly from the northern bean producing state, had agreed in January with the confederation, known as CTM, to sell 380,000 tonnes of beans to the union.
CTM planned to offer its members beans at prices below market levels in what CTM officials said was a way of alleviating family budget pressures.
But the bean farmers said they were promised and expected 6,800 pesos per tonne and were in the end only offered 3,800 per tonne.
Moreover, they claimed CTM's aim was purely political in the run-up to crucial congressional and governorship elections this summer.
CTM is linked to the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, the party of President Ernesto Zedillo.
"Giving away beans at cheap prices is at best a cheap political stunt at worst a means of manipulating poor people," said the bean farm leader who requested anonymity.

CTM officials were not immediately available for comment. A CTM official told Reuters Jan 30 that the beans deal went through in late January and that plans were to sell them at 5.5 pesos per kilo against average market prices of around 7.0 pesos.

But the deal never went ahead as planned. Zacatecas farmers said the first batch of 52 tonnes they planned to sell to CTM has been put in store and that they had even resorted to selling off one-kilo bags in the streets of the capital.
The bean farmers, who do not belong to any organised agricultural group, are not alone in their criticism of CTM.
Mexico's farm debtors group Agrobarzon also slammed the union for trying to gain political mileage out of the cut-price beans idea.

Barzon leader Juan Figueroa told La Jornada daily that they too would start a direct sales program for beans, rice and citrus fruits to the general public. "But it will not be for electioneering reasons," Figueroa said.
